overview: Copper led Tuesday's commodity moves, with LME prices plunging 2.8% to approximately $13,225 per tonne ($6.00 per pound) after a bridge collapse in the Democratic Republic of Congo severed the main transport route from the Kolwezi mining district — the country's copper heartland and the world's second-largest source of the metal. The dollar maintained its grip near 103.5 and the 10-year Treasury yield held above 5.15%, extending the hostile environment for dollar-denominated commodities. Gold fell for a seventh consecutive session to $3,817 per ounce, down 0.9%, extending the weekly decline to approximately 6.5% as hawkish rate expectations continued to weigh on precious metals — silver slipped 0.5% to $46.76. Brent crude staged a modest rebound, rising 0.8% to $93.14, partially recovering from Monday's 3.6% crash as markets found footing ahead of Thursday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen. WTI edged up 0.3% to $86.01. Newcastle coal surged 2.7% to $150 per tonne as approaching winter demand and the ongoing Hormuz-driven LNG supply crisis continued to support thermal fuel. Platinum declined 1.7% to $1,425; palladium eased 0.3% to $965, remaining below the psychologically critical $1,000 level. Cocoa bounced 1.6% to $5,180 on persistent West African supply concerns.

The crypto market continued its slide, with Bitcoin falling approximately 1% to around $64,200 and Ethereum holding near $1,800. The Fear and Greed Index sits at 12 — Extreme Fear. Nvidia reported record Q3 FY2027 revenue of approximately $109 billion after the bell on Tuesday, driven by surging AI data-centre chip demand, though the stock slipped in after-hours trading as investors scrutinised margin compression. Anthropic's IPO priced today at $70–$78 per share (approximately $1 trillion valuation), with trading under ticker ANT beginning Thursday alongside the Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit — a convergence that makes Thursday arguably the most consequential day for markets in months. The November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline is now 9 days away, and the trilateral summit provides the last major diplomatic window. FOMC minutes due at 2 pm ET today. LME base metals were broadly softer — nickel eased 0.4% to $15,790, tin slipped 0.1% to $46,650, and zinc declined 0.5% to $3,680. Grains diverged again — wheat rebounded 1.4% to 595¼ cents on SovEcon's Russian export cut, while corn eased 0.4% to 446¾ cents and soybeans were essentially flat at 1,225½ cents. The DRC bridge collapse adds a new supply disruption to a market already stressed by Hormuz, the gallium deadline, and hawkish monetary policy.

watchItems.title: Bridge collapse in DRC severs main copper transport route from Kolwezi — LME copper down 2.8%
watchItems.text: A bridge collapse in the Democratic Republic of Congo on Tuesday severed the main transport route from the Kolwezi mining district, the country's copper heartland and the world's second-largest source of copper. LME copper plunged 2.8% to approximately $13,225 per tonne ($6.00 per pound) — the steepest daily decline in weeks. The DRC produces approximately 2.5 million tonnes of copper annually, with Kolwezi accounting for a significant share. Emergency road assessments are under way, but alternative routes add substantial time and cost. The disruption comes at a particularly sensitive moment, with the dollar at 103.5 and Treasury yields above 5.15% already pressuring base metals. Copper is a critical input for AI data centres, EVs and electrification — any prolonged supply disruption could tighten an already stressed market.

watchItems.title: Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen tomorrow — gallium deadline, Hormuz and trade all on the agenda
watchItems.text: The unprecedented Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit takes place tomorrow (Thursday, November 19) in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting — the first-ever face-to-face meeting of all three leaders. The agenda reportedly includes denuclearisation, the Iran conflict and Hormuz crisis, trade policy, and potentially the November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony export-control deadline, now 9 days away. Monday's oil crash — Brent down 3.6% — showed markets are already pricing some probability of a diplomatic breakthrough, and Tuesday's modest 0.8% rebound suggests the market is in a holding pattern. For commodity markets, the critical outcomes are whether the trilateral format produces a Hormuz ceasefire framework, any progress on critical mineral export controls, and signals on broader trade policy including the Busan truce.

watchItems.title: Anthropic IPO priced today at $70–$78 per share — trading begins Thursday under ANT at ~$1 trillion valuation
watchItems.text: Anthropic priced its IPO today (Wednesday, November 18) at $70–$78 per share, with trading on the Nasdaq under ticker ANT beginning Thursday, November 19. The offering of 825 million Class A shares implies a fully diluted valuation of up to approximately $1.4 trillion. Orders were approximately six times oversubscribed. A separate private placement sees seven chip-and-cloud suppliers — Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC Partners — buying $26 billion of non-voting Class N shares at the IPO price. The listing coincides with the Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit, making Thursday an extraordinarily dense day for markets. Analysts continue to cite the IPO as a factor draining liquidity from crypto and risk assets as institutional investors reallocate.

watchItems.title: FOMC minutes due today as December rate-hike odds climb to 91% — gold's seventh consecutive decline
watchItems.text: FOMC minutes from the November meeting are due at 2 pm ET today, with markets expecting confirmation of hawkish consensus among policymakers. December rate-hike odds have climbed to approximately 91% for a 25-basis-point increase per Kalshi, up from 88% earlier this week. Gold has now fallen for seven consecutive sessions — its longest losing streak since the Fed pivot last year — dropping to $3,817 per ounce. The 10-year Treasury yield remains above 5.15% and the dollar sits near 103.5, both at or near multi-month highs. The hawkish rate environment continues to weigh broadly on precious metals, with silver at its weakest since late 2025 and palladium stuck below $1,000. If the minutes reveal discussion of a potential 50-basis-point hike in December, gold could face further downside pressure.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: 7th consecutive decline · down ~6.5% over past week · 10Y yield 5.15% · dollar 103.5 · Dec hike odds 91% · FOMC minutes due today
desk.sum: Gold futures settled at $3,817 per ounce on Tuesday, down 0.9%, marking the seventh consecutive decline — the longest losing streak since the Fed pivot last year. Cumulative weekly losses have now extended to approximately 6.5%. The dollar remains firm near 103.5 and the 10-year Treasury yield holds above 5.15%. FOMC minutes due at 2 pm ET today are expected to confirm broad hawkish consensus. CME FedWatch and Kalshi price approximately 91% odds of a 25-basis-point hike at the December 8–9 FOMC, up from 88% earlier this week. Central bank buying at approximately 675 tonnes year to date provides structural support but is insufficient to offset the yield and dollar headwinds. Thursday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen adds event risk.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Lowest since late 2025 · gold-silver ratio above 82 · down ~21% from Oct peak · $48 support broken
desk.sum: Silver slipped 0.5% to $46.76 per ounce on Tuesday, extending losses at the weakest level since late 2025. The gold-silver ratio remains above 82, reflecting silver's continued underperformance versus the broader precious metals complex. Silver is hit by both the rising-yield precious-metal headwind and softening industrial demand sentiment. The break below $47 opens the next support zone around $45.50–$46.00. With the 10-year above 5.15%, the dollar firm, and December rate-hike odds at 91%, the macro environment remains hostile for silver's dual precious-industrial profile. FOMC minutes due today could add further pressure.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $86.01 · modest rebound from Mon crash · market in holding pattern ahead of trilateral summit · 3 US carriers in Gulf · IRGC escalation continues
desk.sum: Brent crude rebounded 0.8% to $93.14 per barrel on Tuesday, partially recovering from Monday's 3.6% crash, with WTI edging up 0.3% to $86.01. The market appears in a holding pattern ahead of Thursday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen, which could produce a Hormuz ceasefire framework and shift the oil supply outlook. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Persian Gulf — the heaviest concentration since 2003. The IRGC's escalation continues with ongoing warnings to shipowners. If the summit disappoints, oil could snap back sharply higher as the ceasefire pricing unwinds; a breakthrough could send Brent towards $85–$88.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME ~$13,225/t · DRC bridge collapse cut Kolwezi route · LME stocks ~329,000t · dollar pressure persistent · AI data-centre demand structural
desk.sum: Copper plunged 2.8% to $6.00 per pound (approximately $13,225 per tonne LME) on Tuesday — the steepest daily decline in weeks — after a bridge collapse in the Democratic Republic of Congo severed the main transport route from the Kolwezi mining district. The DRC is the world's second-largest copper producer, with Kolwezi accounting for a significant share of output. Emergency road assessments are under way. The dollar at 103.5 continues to make dollar-denominated commodities expensive for non-US buyers. LME inventories sit at approximately 329,000 tonnes. AI data-centre, EV and electrification demand remain structural long-term drivers, and any prolonged supply disruption from the DRC could tighten an already stressed market.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Up ~45% YTD · LNG JKM ~$32 · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · winter demand approaching · trilateral summit Thu
desk.sum: Newcastle coal surged 2.7% to $150 per tonne on Tuesday as approaching winter demand and the ongoing Hormuz-driven LNG supply crisis tightened thermal fuel markets. Coal is up approximately 45% year to date. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping approximately 5 bcm of LNG supply offline. The escalation in Hormuz continues with three US carrier strike groups in the Gulf. Thursday's trilateral summit could be a turning point — a Hormuz ceasefire deal would begin to ease energy supply tightness, while a disappointment would reinforce the coal substitution narrative through winter.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Declined further on dollar strength · EV shift weighs on auto catalyst demand · hydrogen electrolysis provides floor
desk.sum: Platinum fell 1.7% to approximately $1,425 per ounce on Tuesday, extending the precious metals slide as the hawkish rate environment and stronger dollar continued to weigh on the complex. Higher borrowing costs, weaker vehicle production and the ongoing shift to EVs continue to pressure automotive catalyst demand — platinum's largest end market. South African mine supply remains constrained by ongoing power issues. Thursday's trilateral summit could shift sentiment if it produces a Hormuz de-escalation framework, which would ease energy costs for PGM-intensive hydrogen electrolysis projects.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Remains below $1,000 · down ~31% YoY · EV transition headwind · weakest since 2018
desk.sum: Palladium eased 0.3% to $965 per ounce on Tuesday, remaining below the psychologically critical $1,000 level after Monday's decisive break. This is the weakest sustained level since 2018. The structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter — remains dominant. With yields above 5.15%, the dollar firm and December rate-hike odds at 91%, the macro environment remains hostile for palladium. Tight South African mine supply offers limited support. Thursday's trilateral summit adds event risk but is unlikely to shift the structural EV headwind.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: IRGC claims 6 ships sunk since weekend · 3 US carriers in Gulf · projectile strike confirmed · trilateral summit Thu · 135+ total incidents
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz crisis remains at elevated levels heading into Thursday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Persian Gulf — the heaviest concentration since 2003. Iran's IRGC claims six vessels have caught fire or sunk since the weekend, and UKMTO confirmed a projectile strike earlier this week. The IRGC Navy continues to warn shipowners against using the American-backed southern route. The trilateral summit provides the most significant diplomatic window to date for a potential Hormuz ceasefire framework. Oil's modest rebound on Tuesday — Brent up 0.8% after Monday's 3.6% crash — suggests markets are in a holding pattern, pricing partial odds of a breakthrough while maintaining a risk premium.
desk.src: The National · gCaptain · UKMTO · Al Jazeera

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: Gave back Monday's gains · dollar headwind persists · WASDE tighter balance sheets supportive · trilateral summit Thu
desk.sum: December corn settled at 446¾ cents per bushel on Tuesday, down 2 cents, giving back a portion of Monday's gains as dollar strength continued to weigh on US export competitiveness. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the November WASDE report continues to provide structural support. Thursday's trilateral summit in Shenzhen could affect trade policy, including the Busan truce soybean commitments and broader grain flows. South American planting continues under generally favourable conditions. The DRC bridge collapse dominated commodity headlines but had limited direct impact on grains.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Rebounded on SovEcon Russia export cut · dollar pressure persists · APEC trade talks Thu
desk.sum: December wheat rebounded 1.4% to 595¼ cents per bushel on Tuesday, recovering from Monday's sell-off. SovEcon's Russian wheat export estimate of 36 million tonnes — below the USDA's 39 million tonne forecast — continued to provide support. The dollar at a 19-month high remains a headwind for US export competitiveness, but tightening global supply estimates offset the pressure. Thursday's APEC summit and the trilateral meeting could address the Abu Dhabi grain corridor, a potential bearish catalyst if stalled Black Sea shipments restart.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: January front-month $12.26 · flat on the day · APEC trade talks could affect soybean commitments
desk.sum: January soybeans settled at $12.26 per bushel (1,225½ cents) on Tuesday, essentially flat on the day as the market held in a narrow range ahead of Thursday's trilateral summit. South American supplies remain more competitive at current exchange rates, and Chinese buying interest is muted ahead of APEC. Thursday's Trump–Xi bilateral could address the Busan truce soybean commitments, which require China to purchase at least 25 million tonnes per year through 2028. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the WASDE report provides a structural floor.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $1,800 · Fear & Greed 12 · Anthropic IPO priced today · no recovery above $65K · $230B wiped since Thu
desk.sum: Bitcoin fell approximately 1% to around $64,200 on Tuesday, failing again to reclaim $65,000. The Fear and Greed Index sits at 12 — Extreme Fear. Ethereum holds near $1,800. Spot Bitcoin ETF outflows continued. Anthropic's IPO pricing today at $70–$78 per share continues to drain institutional liquidity from risk assets, with trading under ANT beginning Thursday. The 10-year yield above 5.15%, the dollar near 20-month highs and contracting stablecoin supply maintain a hostile backdrop. FOMC minutes due today could add further pressure. Key support levels remain $60,000–$62,000 for Bitcoin and $1,750 for Ethereum.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM low $32s · TTF $28 · HH $3.00 · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · trilateral summit Thu pivotal for LNG supply
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) trades near $32 per MMBtu, holding steady as winter demand approaches. TTF sits near $28 per MMBtu, while Henry Hub holds at $3.00. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping approximately 5 bcm offline. The IEA projects 2026 global LNG output will fall about 3%. Thursday's trilateral summit is pivotal — a Hormuz ceasefire framework could begin the process of restoring Qatari LNG flows, while failure would reinforce the supply crisis through winter. Newcastle coal's 2.7% surge to $150 on Tuesday underscores the thermal substitution dynamic.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · IRGC claims 6 ships sunk · 3 carriers in Gulf · trilateral summit Thu · 9 days to Nov 27 deadline
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. The IRGC's claim that six vessels have caught fire or sunk since the weekend continues to constrain Middle Eastern supply logistics. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). Thursday's trilateral summit could be a turning point — a Hormuz ceasefire deal would begin to ease the sulfur supply disruption, while failure would extend the crisis. The November 27 export-control deadline is now 9 days away.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · APEC trade talks Thu · Busan soybean commitment intact
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds at approximately $358 per tonne. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Thursday's APEC summit and trilateral meeting could affect trade policy and fertiliser flows. The Busan trade truce extension to January 10 ensures China's soybean purchase commitments remain intact, supporting underlying grain demand. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 9 days to Nov 27 deadline · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · trilateral summit Thu is last major window
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. The critical catalyst is the November 27 deadline — now 9 days away — when the suspension of China's US-specific export prohibition on antimony expires. Thursday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit provides the last major diplomatic window. The unprecedented three-way format raises hopes for a broader deal. If addressed, Western supply chains could stabilise; if the deadline passes without extension, overseas prices could spike further.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 9 days to Nov 27 deadline · China domestic Ga ~$460/kg · trilateral summit last window · Alcoa Wagerup FID but not producing
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium. Thursday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit provides the last major diplomatic window before the November 27 deadline, now 9 days away. The unprecedented three-way format raises hopes for a broader deal that could include critical mineral supply. China produces about 98% of global gallium. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing. If the bans resume, Western semiconductor and defence industries face renewed supply disruption.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Firmer at $5.30 · upstream tightness in China and Europe · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds at approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, supported by persistent upstream tightness in both China and Europe. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. Thursday's trilateral summit could affect vanadium indirectly if superhard materials restrictions are discussed alongside the November 27 deadline.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Rebounded from Monday's sell-off · ICE inventories elevated · West African supply concerns persist · El Niño risk
desk.sum: ICE cocoa bounced 1.6% to approximately $5,180 per tonne on Tuesday, recovering from Monday's sell-off as persistent supply concerns from West Africa supported prices. Ivory Coast's Sodexam projection that 2026/27 output could drop 21–25% due to an 'exceptionally strong El Niño event' remains a medium-term bullish factor. ICE warehouse inventories remain elevated at multi-year highs, capping upside. The stronger dollar continues to add a headwind for dollar-denominated commodities, but supply fears are increasingly dominant in cocoa's price action.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: Chinese refined cobalt futures ¥230,000–240,000/t · Rotterdam $17–18/lb · sentiment improving but fundamentals weak
desk.sum: Cobalt is estimated near $35,000 per tonne, with Chinese refined cobalt futures in the ¥230,000–240,000 per tonne range. Rotterdam standard-grade cobalt metal sits at $17–18 per pound. The recovery from early November's lows appears driven by sentiment and capital inflows rather than a fundamental shift, with downstream buyers still purchasing on a need basis. The DRC's bridge collapse on Tuesday, while primarily affecting copper routes, could have secondary effects on cobalt logistics from the same mining region. The NMC-to-LFP battery chemistry shift continues to weigh on the structural demand outlook.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: New one-year low · structural oversupply persists · Goldman: 444k t global surplus by 2028 · supply ramp-up continues
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures slipped to ¥89,000 per tonne, marking a fresh one-year low. Supply ramp-up continues to outpace demand growth, with new mine restarts adding capacity. Goldman Sachs projects a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Lithium's inability to rally despite broader commodity volatility underscores the structural oversupply challenge. Thursday's trilateral summit is not expected to have a direct lithium impact.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · oil rebound marginal for synthetic costs
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), range-bound. Southeast Asian supply remains tight, with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Tuesday's modest oil rebound had limited impact on synthetic rubber production costs. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. The stronger dollar at a 19-month high remains a headwind for dollar-denominated commodities.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Spot steady ~$91 · long-term contracts near $99/lb · IAEA: 78 reactors under construction · AI data-centre demand structural
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds at approximately $91 per pound U₃O₈, with long-term contract prices continuing to climb near record US levels of $99 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. The IAEA counts 78 reactors under construction worldwide and has raised its outlook for global nuclear capacity. Kazatomprom's TQZ sulphuric acid plant delays continue to limit leaching capacity. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver, with Meta, Amazon and Microsoft having signed nuclear power agreements. Thursday's trilateral summit could touch on nuclear arms control, though direct market impact is expected to be limited.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: Ex-China NdPr $109–121/kg FOB · CIF Rotterdam $100–120/kg · Nov 10 broader controls deadline passed · Nov 27 deadline 9 days
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide trades near $72 per kilogram domestically in China, while ex-China prices sit at $109–121 per kilogram FOB, down $3 per kilogram. CIF Rotterdam ranges $100–120 per kilogram. Heavy rare earths remain tighter, with ex-China dysprosium oxide at $3,300–4,200 per kilogram. The November 10 deadline for broader controls has passed without a published extension. The November 27 US-specific deadline for gallium, germanium and antimony — now 9 days away — adds further uncertainty. Thursday's trilateral summit provides a diplomatic window for critical mineral discussions.
desk.src: SMM · Rare Earth Exchanges · Benchmark Minerals

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · miners holding firm pricing stance · CIF China flat
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. Miners continue holding a firm pricing stance, with Comilog (Gabonese lumps) at $4.50 per mtu and Consolidated Minerals (Australian 46% lumps) at $4.80 per mtu. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The forward cost picture provides support, but soft downstream consumption limits gains.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Eased modestly · dollar pressure · Indonesia RKAB quota tightening provides some support · surplus persists
desk.sum: LME nickel eased 0.4% to $15,790 per tonne on Tuesday, a modest decline amid broader base metals weakness driven by copper's DRC bridge collapse. The dollar at 103.5 continues to weigh on the market. Indonesia's potential tightening of RKAB mining quotas provides a modest floor, but the global nickel surplus persists as Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions continue. Thursday's trilateral summit and APEC trade talks add uncertainty. The macro environment remains hostile with yields above 5.15% and December rate-hike odds at 91%.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Eased from $48,295 cash · LME backwardation still wide · cancelled warrants elevated · Myanmar ban constraining supply
desk.sum: LME tin eased marginally to approximately $46,650 per tonne on Tuesday, holding relatively firm compared to copper's sharp sell-off. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. The LME backwardation remains wide, signalling tight near-term supply. Cancelled warrants are elevated, suggesting further inventory drawdowns ahead. Tin continues to outperform the base metals complex on its significantly tighter fundamental supply position.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: TCs deeply negative · LME stocks declining · smelter curtailments continue · up ~23% YoY despite recent weakness
desk.sum: LME zinc declined 0.5% to $3,680 per tonne on Tuesday, pulled lower by the broader base metals sell-off triggered by copper's DRC bridge collapse. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments. LME inventories have been declining, continuing the drawdown trend. The structural supply deficit remains intact, but the combination of yields above 5.15%, the dollar surge and soft downstream consumption caps near-term upside. Zinc is up approximately 23% year-over-year despite recent weakness. Thursday's APEC outcomes could shift sentiment for base metals broadly.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,750 · China FOB $1,845 · Western ~3.5x China · 9 days to Nov 27 deadline · trilateral summit last window
desk.sum: European tungsten APT firmed to $2,750 per mtu in Rotterdam, up from $2,725, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu. Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels. The November 27 deadline for the US-specific ban is now 9 days away. Thursday's trilateral summit provides the last major diplomatic window. The unprecedented Trump–Xi–Putin format raises hopes for a broader deal that could include tungsten alongside gallium, germanium and antimony. The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · IRGC escalation raises stakes · trilateral summit Thu
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Gulf — the heaviest military concentration since 2003. QatarEnergy's Ras Laffan facility repairs remain estimated at 3–5 years. Thursday's trilateral summit could be pivotal for helium if it produces a Hormuz ceasefire framework — Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium, and any path to restoring Ras Laffan operations would need Hormuz de-escalation. Russia's export controls extend through 2027.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · wheat rebound supportive for fertiliser demand
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. Tuesday's grain divergence — wheat rebounding 1.4% while corn and soybeans eased — produced a mixed near-term fertiliser demand signal. Thursday's APEC summit could affect trade flows. The ongoing Hormuz attacks further reduce the probability of Middle Eastern sulfur supply normalising, keeping the cost structure elevated.
